questions.q: If a recipe for 2 people uses 3 spoons of salt, what is the ratio of people to salt?
questions.a: The ratio is 2:3. A student might incorrectly write 3:2, which shows they are confusing the order of the quantities being compared.

questions.q: If you have a map with a scale of 1:500, what does that "1" represent compared to the "500"?
questions.a: The "1" represents a unit on the map (like 1 cm), while the "500" represents 500 of that same unit on the ground. A student answering "1 cm is 500 meters" shows they have not yet understood that the units must be the same before conversion.

questions.q: A juice mix is made with 2 parts orange to 5 parts water. If you use 6 cups of orange juice, how many cups of water do you need?
questions.a: You need 15 cups of water. Step 1: Identify ratio 2:5. Step 2: Notice 6 is 3 times 2. Step 3: Multiply 5 by 3 to get 15. A student answering 9 might have added 3 to the 5 instead of multiplying, missing the multiplicative nature of ratios.

questions.q: Are the ratios 3:4 and 9:12 equivalent? Why or why not?
questions.a: Yes, they are equivalent. If you multiply both terms of 3:4 by 3, you get 9:12. A student saying "no" might be looking at the numbers as individual values rather than as a relationship that can be scaled.

questions.q: If a building design has a length-to-width ratio of 4:2, is a building of 8m by 6m proportional to this design?
questions.a: No. The design ratio simplifies to 2:1, but 8:6 simplifies to 4:3. A student saying "yes" is likely just looking for "bigger numbers" without checking if the multiplier is the same for both dimensions.

questions.q: Create a real-life scenario where a ratio of 1:10 is used and explain why.
questions.a: A good answer would be a drink concentrate (1 part syrup to 10 parts water) or a scale drawing (1 cm on paper to 10 cm in real life). A poor answer would just provide two numbers without a context or a clear "part-to-part" relationship.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Ratio is a ______ way to compare two quantities of the same kind by division, showing how many times one quantity contains the other.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are baking a cake for your family of 4, and the ______ calls for 2 cups of sugar.
What is Ratio? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Ratio is a mathematical way to compare two quantities of the same kind by division, showing how many times one quantity contains the other.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Ratio?
questions.a: Students often use addition instead of multiplication when solving proportions.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to identify, set up, and solve problems involving scaling quantities (like ingredients in a recipe or distances on a map) using the concept of equivalent ratios.
